summary: Sets out requirements for a video codec designed mainly for use over the internet, and describes an evaluation methodology for measuring compression efficiency to decide whether the requirements are met.

plainLanguage.summary: Before building a new way to squash videos, you write down what it must do and how to test it fairly. This is that list.

subtitle: Specifies requirements for internet video codecs and how to measure if they meet them.

tldr.problem: Before building a new video codec for internet use, the codec community needed a shared understanding of what the codec must achieve and how to fairly test whether it succeeds, covering applications from streaming to videoconferencing to surveillance.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines general, basic, and optional requirements for coding efficiency, complexity, scalability, and error resilience; then describes an evaluation methodology using rate-distortion curves aligned between reference codecs (like HEVC/H.265) and candidate codecs, measuring compression gain with BD-rate metrics.
tldr.outcome: The NETVC working group used this document to guide development of modern video codecs. The requirements and methodology ensure new codecs deliver meaningful compression improvements over existing standards while remaining implementable.

facts.label: Compression efficiency target
facts.value: At least 25% BD-rate savings over HEVC/H.265 and VP9

facts.label: Subrange target
facts.value: At least 15% BD-rate savings in each bitrate range

today: RFC 8761 is an Informational RFC published in April 2020. It remains the definitive requirements document and evaluation methodology guide for internet video codec development, used by codec projects and standards bodies including the IETF NETVC working group.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The RFC addresses requirements for video codecs designed mainly for internet use. Unlike standards for a single application, internet video covers many use cases: on-demand streaming of movies, live video conferencing with tight delay constraints, interactive video sharing, screencasting with computer-generated content, game streaming, and video surveillance.

Each use case has different demands. Streaming can tolerate seconds of delay and use complex offline encoders. Videoconferencing must keep delay below 100 milliseconds. Surveillance cameras have limited processing power. The RFC catalogs these requirements, defines what a codec must do, and explains how to measure whether it succeeds fairly.
sections.plainLanguage: Different video uses need different tradeoffs. A movie can wait for encoding, but a video call cannot. This document lists all the uses and what each one needs.

sections.title: Core Requirements
sections.content:
The general requirements include coding efficiency: new codecs must deliver at least 25% bitrate savings compared to state-of-the-art codecs like HEVC/H.265 and VP9. The codec must support profiles and levels (subsets of features and complexity limits) so devices know what they can decode. The bitstream must allow extensibility and backward compatibility: new features can be added without breaking older decoders.

Basic requirements include support for 8 to 10 bit depth per color component, color formats like YCbCr 4:2:0 and 4:4:4, low-delay encoding modes for real-time applications, temporal (frame-rate) scalability, and error resilience mechanisms so frames can be partially recovered if packets are lost.

Optional but desirable requirements include support for wider color gamuts, 12-bit depth, scalability with low overhead, and tools that help parallel processing on multicore devices.
sections.plainLanguage: The codec must squash video much better than old ones. It must work in low-delay video calls. It should handle lots of colors and work on many devices.

sections.title: Internet Video Applications
sections.content:
The RFC describes seven main applications. Internet Video Streaming (movies, TV, animation) uses adaptive bitrate encoding at multiple resolutions; encoding happens in the cloud, one time, in parallel. IPTV (TV over IP networks) requires fast random access points (1 to 5 seconds) for channel switching. Video Conferencing needs end-to-end delays under 320 milliseconds (preferably under 100 ms) and error robustness for packet loss.

Video Sharing (user-generated content like YouTube) needs random access for seeking and resolution/quality scalability. Screencasting demands efficient compression of computer-generated content with sharp edges and full resolution. Game Streaming requires low latency (under 100 ms turnaround for user input) and handling of fast motion. Video Surveillance needs low encoder complexity for resource-limited cameras and support for monochrome and wide dynamic range.
sections.plainLanguage: A live video call needs speed. A movie can wait. A security camera cannot waste power. This section lists what each video use really needs.

sections.title: Evaluation Methodology
sections.content:
The RFC defines a rigorous evaluation process. Testing occurs at ten bitrate points across three overlapping ranges: low bitrate range (LBR), medium bitrate range (MBR), and high bitrate range (HBR). For each bitrate, quantization parameter (QP) values must be aligned between the reference codec (HEVC or VP9) and the candidate codec so quality levels match.

Quality is measured using two metrics: PSNR (Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio, measuring pixel accuracy) and MS-SSIM (Multi-Scale Structural Similarity, measuring human-perceived quality). Results are plotted as rate-distortion curves. The BD-rate (Bjontegaard Delta Rate) metric then calculates average bitrate savings across the curves. A candidate codec must achieve at least 25% BD-rate savings overall and 15% savings in each bitrate subrange.

Subjective evaluation using Mean Opinion Score (MOS) testing is also required for final adoption. Test sequences are defined in a companion document.
sections.plainLanguage: Line up both codecs at the same quality levels, measure how much smaller the file is, then calculate the average savings. Must be at least 25% smaller overall.

sections.title: Profiles, Levels, and Deployment
sections.content:
The RFC specifies example profiles (tier 1, tier 2, tier 3) with different bit depths and color formats. Levels define maximum picture sizes and frame rates; 13 levels are suggested, ranging from 128x96 at 30 fps up to 8192x4320 at 120 fps. These constraints help implementations manage decoder complexity and memory.

Bitstream syntax should allow easy parsing at the header level without needing to decode the entire frame to identify packet components, supporting efficient packetization and error recovery. The codec should define a hypothetical reference decoder (HRD) buffer model to help implementations manage data flow.
sections.plainLanguage: Different devices handle different video sizes. Small phones get lower resolution profiles, big TVs get higher ones. Each level says what is the biggest, fastest video it must handle.
